entities.name: Amerigo Vespucci
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Amerigo Vespucci (c. 1454 – March 3, 1512) was an Italian merchant, explorer, and cartographer from the Republic of Florence, whose name became eponymously linked to the "New World" through a cartographic convention. His meticulously documented voyages along the eastern coast of South America, particularly between 1499 and 1502, provided compelling geographical and observational evidence that these lands constituted a distinct continent, separate from Asia. This profound conceptual shift fundamentally redefined the global understanding of geography among Europeans and spurred subsequent exploration and colonial ambitions.

Vespucci's most impactful contribution stemmed from his third voyage (1501–1502), undertaken under the patronage of King Manuel I of Portugal. Sailing south from the Cape Verde Islands, he meticulously charted a significant stretch of the Brazilian coast, reaching as far as modern-day Patagonia. His detailed observations of the vast continental coastline, its diverse flora and fauna, and the indigenous populations convinced him that this landmass was too extensive and geographically distinct to be part of Asia. These insights were articulated in his widely circulated letters, notably *Mundus Novus* (1503), which dramatically announced the discovery of a "New World." He also served as *piloto mayor* (chief navigator) for Spain from 1508, training navigators and compiling maps at the Casa de Contratación in Seville.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Amerigo Vespucci's conceptualization of the Americas as a distinct 'New World' fundamentally reshaped European cartography and understanding of global geography, directly leading to the continents being named after him. His detailed accounts spurred further exploration and colonization, irrevocably altering world history.
